$comment: How WiredMind sounds in each language. `pnpm i18n:draft` gives the translator the shared rules and the language's own notes; reviewers can sharpen a language here.
shared: Readers are students aged about 11 to 16 and their teachers. Write the way a good science teacher talks to a class: short sentences, plain words, one idea at a time. Keep the English's warmth and its honesty about what is simplified.

Keep every scientific term from the glossary exactly as given (inflect it as the grammar needs). In lesson copy each <term> keeps the scientific name and its <gloss> is a short, friendly nickname in parentheses: three words or fewer where the language allows.

Buttons are named in lesson text: 'Tap Stimulate', 'silence the Kenyon cells'. Use exactly your translations of viewer.controls.stimulate, viewer.controls.silence, and viewer.lesson.cueSwitchOn for them, so the words on screen match the words in the lesson.
Keep the colors (orange, yellow, blue, pink, green, violet) and what each one names; students match them to the screen.
Keep every number as digits (0-9), with your language's usual decimal and thousands separators. Keep units (ms, mV, Hz) as symbols.
Never translate the brand WiredMind, the names in the glossary's keep list, cell type codes (LC4, LPLC2, P-EN2, E-PG), or anything inside {curly braces}.
Keep every <tag> and </tag> exactly, around the words that mean the same thing in your sentence. A link tag may move anywhere its words go.
Use your language's own quotation marks and punctuation, and non-breaking spaces where its typography wants them.

Page titles (meta.*.title, meta.lessonTitle, meta.notFoundTitle) must stay within 60 characters and descriptions within 155, after the placeholders are filled; count a Chinese, Japanese, or Korean character as two. Write them for search results: say what the page is and why it is worth a click.

locales.he: Modern Hebrew without niqqud. Address students in the plural imperative (לחצו, שלחו, צפו), which reads as gender-neutral in Israeli classrooms. Hebrew quotation marks "…" and gershayim in abbreviations (מ״מ). Latin names and units stay in Latin script.
locales.ar: Modern Standard Arabic that a secondary-school student in any Arab country reads easily. Address the student with the singular imperative (اضغط، أرسل، شاهد) as the neutral classroom form. Western digits (0-9), Arabic comma (،) and question mark (؟). Latin names and units stay in Latin script.
locales.es: Neutral Spanish that reads naturally in both Spain and Latin America; avoid regional slang and vosotros. Address students with tú. Use «…» or "…" consistently.
locales.fr: French for collège and lycée. Lessons and the viewer address the student with tu; the landing page, the about page, and the teachers' section use vous. Typographic spaces before : ; ? ! and inside « … ». Respect accents on capitals (É, À).
locales.de: German for Schülerinnen und Schüler. Lessons and the viewer use du; the landing page, the about page, and the teachers' section use Sie. Quotation marks „…“. Prefer established German terms; English loanwords only where German science classes use them (Gap Junctions).
locales.pt-BR: Brazilian Portuguese with você throughout. Use "…" quotation marks. Prefer terms a Brazilian biology textbook would use.
locales.ru: Russian for school students. Lessons and the viewer use ты; the landing page, the about page, and the teachers' section use вы. Quotation marks «…», the long dash —, and the letter ё where it matters for reading.
locales.zh-CN: Simplified Chinese for mainland middle and high school students. Address the reader as 你. Full-width punctuation (，。：；！？“”（）), no spaces between Chinese characters, one space around Latin words and numbers is optional; stay consistent.
locales.ja: Japanese in です・ます style. Lessons use gentle instructions (〜してください, 〜してみましょう). Full-width punctuation (、。「」（）). Use the katakana and kanji terms from the glossary.
locales.ko: Korean in polite 해요체 throughout. Use the glossary terms; add the English in parentheses only where a Korean student would not know the term.
locales.hi: Standard Hindi in Devanagari that a CBSE secondary student reads easily. Use आप. Where Indian classrooms say the English-origin word (न्यूरॉन, सिग्नल), use it rather than a rare Sanskrit coinage. Western digits (0-9).
locales.it: Italian for scuola media and superiore, addressing the student with tu throughout. Quotation marks «…».
locales.tr: Turkish for ortaokul and lise. Lessons and the viewer use sen; the landing page, the about page, and the teachers' section use siz. Mind the dotted and dotless i in capitals (İ, I).
locales.pl: Polish for szkoła podstawowa and liceum. Lessons and the viewer use ty; site pages use neutral, impersonal forms. Quotation marks „…”.
locales.nl: Dutch with je and jij throughout, as Dutch websites do. Prefer established Dutch terms; English loanwords only where Dutch biology classes use them.
locales.id: Bahasa Indonesia. Lessons and the viewer address the student with kamu; the landing page, the about page, and the teachers' section use Anda.
locales.vi: Vietnamese for trung học students. Address the reader as bạn. Use full diacritics.
